# I'll write the story directly to answer.txt
story = '''RIBBIT! Settle down, little pollywogs, and let old Grandfather Toad tell you how the Great Pond came to be.

Long ago, before your gills had even formed, there was a time of the Tyrant Heron. A vast shadow that demanded tribute from every creature of the marsh. Each frog, each newt, each water beetle had to bring offerings or face the sharp beak of judgment.

But the pond creatures discovered something powerful.

It began with three brave souls: Whisker the Catfish, Thornback the Turtle, and Glimmer the Dragonfly. They could not have been more different—one swam the depths, one carried fortress armor, one danced on iridescent wings above the water. Yet they gathered at the Great Lily Pad Council, not as rulers and subjects, but as equals.

"We cannot defeat the Heron alone," said Whisker, her whiskers twitching with ancient wisdom. "But together, each contributing what only they can contribute..."

Thornback nodded slowly. "I can carry stones. Build walls."

Glimmer's wings hummed. "I can see everything from above. I can be the eyes."

And so began the building of the Great Cattail Engines—magnificent machines of reed and vine and clever knots. No single creature designed them. The beavers contributed engineering knowledge passed through generations. The water striders wove the delicate trigger mechanisms. The crayfish dug the foundation trenches with their powerful claws.

Each creature chose their role freely. No whip, no decree, no crown commanded them. They worked because they understood: the pond belongs to those who tend it.

When the Tyrant Heron finally descended to collect tribute, the marsh was ready.

Glimmer spotted the shadow falling across the water and flashed her wings in the signal. The Cattail Engines roared to life—great nets of woven reed launching upward, powered by the tension of a thousand willing workers. Thornback led the shield wall, his ancient shell now reinforced with the combined work of generations. Whisker coordinated from below, her voice carrying through the water to every creature who needed to hear.

The Heron, confronted not with an army that followed orders, but with a community that followed conscience, retreated to find easier prey elsewhere.

That night, the creatures of the marsh did not crown a king. They did not build a throne. They simply returned to their lives—fishing, swimming, raising their young in the safety they had created together.

And this is what I want you to understand, my beloved tadpoles: the pond works because WE make it work. When a family of frogs needs help building their spawn nest, neighbors arrive with mud and reeds—not because a law compels them, but because that is who we choose to be. When the water grows stagnant, the strongest swimmers dig new channels—not for reward, but because clean water serves everyone, including themselves.

We have no kings because we need none. We have no queens because we are all sovereign over our own lives. Every voice matters in the Lily Pad Council. Every creature contributes according to their ability and receives according to their need.

The herons still hunt beyond our waters. The raccoons still prowl the banks. We do not hate them—they follow their nature, as we follow ours. But we do not bow to them, and we do not let them rule us.

You, little ones, with your wriggling tails and your wide golden eyes, are inheritors of this great work. Not inheritors of a throne, but inheritors of a responsibility: to think for yourself, to care for your neighbors, to trust that freedom and cooperation are not opposites but the very same thing.

The pond is ours because we are the pond.

Now, who wants to hear about the time we built the Great Filter Dam to stop the poison runoff from the Two-Legs' fields? That one involves a very clever water snake and what we call the Silt-Sifter 3000...'''

with open('answer.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(story)

print("Story written to answer.txt")
